task_title: Elements of Effective Teaching in a Professional Environment
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain the five aviation instructor responsibilities, the extra duties of a flight instructor including supervising learners in the airplane and on paper, the qualifications, professionalism, professional development and ethics expected of a CFI, and show all of them while you deliver a lesson the examiner assigns.
why: Learners look to their instructor as a role model, so how you behave teaches as much as what you say [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]. The FAA places full responsibility for student flight training on the CFI [[1:38|PHAK 1-23]], and every endorsement you sign is a legal and ethical judgment the FAA may hold you accountable for [[25:184|AIH 9-14]].

prereading.label: AIH 8-1 to 8-4
prereading.what: The five aviation instructor responsibilities: helping learners, adequate instruction, standards of performance, emphasizing the positive and minimizing learner frustration.

prereading.label: AIH 8-5 to 8-12
prereading.what: Flight instructor responsibilities, the Aviator's Model Code of Conduct, safety by example, qualifications, professionalism and professional development.

prereading.label: AIH 5-1 to 5-4
prereading.what: The four essential teaching skills, the instructor's code of ethics and the Flight Instructors Model Code of Conduct (FIMCC).

prereading.label: AIH 9-8 to 9-9
prereading.what: How much control to use during learner practice, and the positive exchange of flight controls.

prereading.label: AIH 9-11 to 9-14
prereading.what: See and avoid, first solo, post-solo debriefing, pilot supervision and practical test recommendations.

prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.183 to 61.199
prereading.what: Flight instructor eligibility, records, privileges, limitations, recent experience and reinstatement. Read 61.189, 61.193, 61.195 and 61.197 closely.

prereading.label: AC 61-65K 26 to 30
prereading.what: Flight instructor certification, the Gold Seal certificate and the ways to establish flight instructor recent experience.

warmup: Think first: think back to the best and the worst instructor you ever flew with. Write down three things each one did. How many of the six were about flying skill, and how many were about how they treated you, prepared, explained and kept their word?

key_terms.def: The established standards in the appropriate ACS or PTS that an instructor trains every applicant to, in all subject areas, procedures and maneuvers [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].
The AIH stresses that the ACS/PTS is a testing document, not a teaching document. Lesson standards build gradually to reach or exceed it [[25:160|AIH 8-2]] [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].
The flight instructor's guidance and restraint over a learner's solo operations. The AIH calls it by far the most important flight instructor responsibility [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

A three-step spoken handover: 'You have the flight controls,' 'I have the flight controls,' 'You have the flight controls,' with a visual check, so there is never doubt about who is flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

The instructor's signed recommendation on the application for a certificate or rating. It should follow a thorough demonstration that is never less than the complete ACS procedure [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

A logbook or training record entry by an authorized instructor. It may be customized but must at least cite the 14 CFR part 61 section completed; samples are in AC 61-65 Appendix A [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].
What a flight instructor must accomplish within the preceding 24 calendar months to exercise instructor privileges, such as a practical test, a pass-rate record or a FIRC [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(a)]].

An FAA-approved course of ground training, flight training or both. Completing one within the preceding 3 calendar months is one way to establish recent experience [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(b)(2)(iii)]].

A flight instructor certificate with a distinctive gold seal, issued to instructors who keep a high level of training activity and meet special criteria, such as a strong first-time pass rate [[12:24|AC 61-65K 28]].

key_terms.term: Flight Instructors Model Code of Conduct (FIMCC)
key_terms.def: A peer-reviewed code that offers a vision of flight education excellence and recommended practices to improve the quality and safety of instruction [[25:107|AIH 5-4]].
Broad guidance for general aviation pilots in seven sections. Its principles complement and supplement what is merely legal; it is not a standard [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].
Keeping the highest level of knowledge, training and currency through lifelong learning, and also behaving in a professional manner [[25:165|AIH 8-7]].

f1.caption: Figure 8-1. There are five main responsibilities of aviation instructors. (AIH 8-1)
f1.alt: A boxed list titled Responsibilities of All Aviation Instructors: helping learners learn, providing adequate instruction, demanding appropriate standards of performance, emphasizing the positive, and ensuring aviation safety.

f2.caption: Figure 8-4. These are practical ways to minimize learner frustration. (AIH 8-4)
f2.alt: A boxed list titled Minimizing Learner Frustration: motivate learners, keep learners informed, approach learners as individuals, give credit when due, criticize constructively, be consistent, admit errors.

f3.caption: Figure 8-5. The flight instructor has many additional responsibilities. (AIH 8-5)
f3.alt: A boxed list titled Additional Responsibilities of Flight Instructors with eight items: evaluation of learner piloting ability, pilot supervision, practical test recommendations, flight instructor endorsements, additional training and endorsements, pilot proficiency, see and avoid responsibility, and learner's pre-solo flight thought process.

f4.caption: Figure 8-6. Teaching tips from veteran flight instructors. (AIH 8-7)
f4.alt: A numbered list of twelve tips, including rehearsing preflight briefings on video, finding a mentor for a second opinion before critical phases such as first solo, 'just because it's legal, doesn't make it safe', documenting training as though the NTSB were going to read it, encouraging personal minimums and reviewing NTSB accident reports.

f5.caption: Figure 8-7. Guidelines for an aviation instructor. (AIH 8-8)
f5.alt: Two boxed lists. Instructor Do's has sixteen items such as be professional at all times, be sincere, maintain a calm demeanor, avoid profanity, define common terms, continue professional development and admit errors. Instructor Don'ts has ten items such as ridicule the learner's performance, model irresponsible flight behaviors, say one thing but do another, demand unreasonable progress and correct errors without an explanation.

f6.caption: Figure 9-8. Positive exchange of flight controls. A visual check is recommended, the learner returns control the same way, and there should never be any doubt about who is flying the aircraft. (AIH 9-9)
f6.alt: Three stacked green boxes titled Positive Exchange of Flight Controls. One: when the instructor wants the learner to take control, the instructor says 'You have the flight controls.' Two: the learner acknowledges immediately, 'I have the flight controls.' Three: the instructor again says 'You have the flight controls.'

chunks.title: The five responsibilities, starting with helping learners

body.p: The AIH sums up the job in one line: an aviation instructor transfers knowledge. Instructors help learners meet and exceed established standards, measure their performance against those standards, and give positive reinforcement along the way [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

The ACS lists five aviation instructor responsibilities: helping learners, providing adequate instruction, training to established standards of performance, emphasizing the positive, and minimizing learner frustrations. The AIH text teaches each one under matching headings [[25:159|AIH 8-1]] [[25:160|AIH 8-2]] [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]. Its Figure 8-1 shows 'ensuring aviation safety' where the ACS has minimizing learner frustrations [[25:159|AIH 8-1]], so know both lists.
Helping learners. The AIH makes four points:

bullets: Helping learners starts with learning being enjoyable. A pleasurable lesson keeps motivation high, but you never sacrifice standards to make things easy [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].
Leading people to learning by making it easy is a fallacy. Learners may be drawn to easy tasks at first, but they put more effort into activities that bring rewards [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].
Standards, and measuring against them, are key to helping learners. People want to feel capable and are proud of reaching difficult goals [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

Learning should be interesting. Knowing the objective of each period gives it meaning for learner and instructor alike. Not knowing it leads to confusion, disinterest and uneasiness [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

callout.text: Application: open every lesson with the objective in one sentence and what 'good' will look like today. It costs 30 seconds and removes the uneasiness the AIH warns about [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

check.q: Does helping learners mean making each lesson easy?
check.a: No. Make it enjoyable and interesting, but keep the standard. Meeting a challenging standard is what gives learners satisfaction [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

body.p: Providing adequate instruction means tailoring your teaching to the person in front of you. Analyze the learner's personality, thinking and ability, because no two learners are alike and one method will not work equally well for all [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]. Talk with the learner at some length about background, interests, temperament and way of thinking, and be ready to change methods as training advances [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

head: Learner
The trap
What the AIH says to do
rows: Quiet and reserved
You may decide they are a slow learner when they actually lack self-confidence and fail to act at the right time even though they understand [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]
Direct instruction at building self-confidence rather than more drill on fundamentals [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]
Timid
Too much criticism discourages a timid person, while brisk instruction may push a different learner to work harder [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]
Match the amount of criticism to the person [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]
Needs more time
Too much help and encouragement can build a feeling of incompetence [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]
Combine tact, keen perception and delicate handling [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]
Slow progress from discouragement
Goals feel out of reach [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]
Assign more easily attained goals. Split the task into elements, for example S-turns with headings only first, then altitude, drift correction and coordination one at a time [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]
Fast learner
Makes few mistakes, may think correcting errors is unimportant, and overconfidence leads to faulty performance [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]
Keep raising the standard each lesson and demand greater effort. Never invent deficiencies; unfair criticism immediately destroys confidence in you [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]

body.p: In some ways you are a practical psychologist. You meet that duty by knowing the fundamentals of instructing and by careful analysis of, and continuing interest in, each learner [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]. Watch one habit in yourself: most new instructors adopt the methods their own instructors used, or the way they themselves learn best. Having learned that way does not mean it was the best way, so stay open-minded and seek other resources [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

callout.text: Individuals learn only if they are aware of their errors, and skills are retained better by learners who analyze their own performance [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]. Letting a fast learner's small errors slide is not kindness.

check.q: A quiet learner sees the unstable approach but hesitates to call the go-around. More drill, or something else?
check.a: Something else. The AIH example says to aim instruction at self-confidence rather than drill on flight fundamentals [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

chunks.title: Training to established standards of performance

body.p: Training to established standards of performance means you train each applicant to the standards in all subject areas, procedures and maneuvers in every task of every area of operation in the appropriate ACS or PTS [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]. How you use those standards matters as much as knowing them:

bullets: The ACS/PTS is a testing document, not a teaching document [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]. The focus of training is learning and understanding why the standards exist and how they were set [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].
Do not focus lessons on the minimum acceptable standard for passing. Lesson completion standards should gradually reach or exceed the ACS before final checkride preparation [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].
Meeting the standard provides only a limited margin of safety, so teach why pilots are trained to standards and how the standards are set [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].
Certification tests cover the most critical job tasks and do not represent a whole syllabus. Do not limit your objectives to the minimum published requirements [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

When you evaluate, use the established standards suitably modified for the learner's experience and stage of development, and judge mastery of each element, not just the overall result [[25:168|AIH 8-10]].

callout.text: The ACS is the finish line, not the lesson plan. Teach past it, test to it [[25:160|AIH 8-2]] [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

body.p: The PHAK makes the same point from the learner's side: practical tests are a sampling of pilot ability compressed into a short period, and the instructor's goal is to train the 'total' pilot [[1:39|PHAK 1-24]].

check.q: Why not grade lesson 3 of a private course against the ACS tolerances?
check.a: The ACS is a testing tool. Lesson standards are set for the learner's stage and build gradually until they reach or exceed the ACS [[25:168|AIH 8-10]] [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

body.p: Emphasizing the positive starts with you. The way you conduct yourself and the attitudes you show make an impression, and teaching in a way that gives learners a positive image of aviation adds to your success [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

The AIH ties this to the learning process: a negative self-concept inhibits perception, fear hurts perception, feeling threatened limits it, and negative motivation is weaker than positive motivation. Knowing this is not enough; you have to detect these feelings in learners and stop them from undermining instruction [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

head: First lesson
What the learner hears
rows: Built negatively (AIH example)

Preflight taught as a guard against disastrous emergencies, taxiing as a way to lose control, stalls as how so many people lose their lives, and forced landings on day one. The learner may wonder if learning to fly is a good idea [[25:161|AIH 8-3]]
Built positively (AIH example)

Preflight to get acquainted with the aircraft, then a perfectly normal flight to a nearby airport and back. Afterward, point out how easy the trip was and that nothing critical happened or was expected [[25:161|AIH 8-3]]

body.p: This does not remove stalls and emergencies from training. Introduce them after the learner is acquainted with normal operations, following a syllabus that builds a foundation, so they are less discouraging, less frightening and do not block learning through fear [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

callout.text: Positive instruction results in positive learning. A learner's failure to perform often results from the instructor's inability to transfer the information [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

body.p: Nothing in aviation demands that learners suffer. Keep training flexible and change the method when a learner has trouble grasping a task [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

check.q: Does emphasizing the positive mean skipping stall training for nervous learners?
check.a: No. Stalls and emergencies stay in the syllabus; they come after the learner is familiar with normal operations [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

body.p: Minimizing learner frustrations in the classroom or the airplane is the instructor's responsibility [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]. Lesson plans in an organized curriculum help: most pilots do not want to be learners, so being able to measure progress and 'see an end in sight' cuts frustration and raises motivation [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

head: Rule
Why it matters
What you do
rows: Motivate learners
More is gained from wanting to learn than from being forced to [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Show the benefit and purpose of each lesson; enjoyment and effort go up [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Keep learners informed
Learners feel insecure when they do not know what is expected of them or what will happen [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Give a course overview, keep them posted on progress, and give adequate notice of exams and assignments [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Approach learners as individuals
Teaching only to the group aims at an average personality that fits no one [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Remember each person in a class has a unique personality [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Give credit when due
Good work that goes unnoticed frustrates [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Praise when deserved. Praise given too freely becomes valueless [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Criticize constructively
'Unsatisfactory' with no explanation frustrates, and errors not identified are perpetuated through faulty practice [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Brief the error and how to correct it [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Be consistent
If the same thing is fine one day and wrong the next, the learner is confused [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Keep your philosophy and actions consistent [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Admit errors
Learners sense a cover-up or bluff quickly, and it destroys their confidence [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Acknowledge mistakes honestly; if in doubt, admit it [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]

check.q: Your learner flies her best crosswind landing yet and you say nothing because 'that is the standard.' Which rule did you miss?
check.a: Give credit when due. Learners expect their good work to be noticed, and deserved praise is an incentive to do even better [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

body.p: Flight instructor responsibilities go beyond the five above because your learners will fly. Learning to fly should be a habit-building period, and the flight instructor's job is to 'mold' the learner into a safe pilot who takes a professional approach to flying. More flight instructor duties are in 14 CFR part 61 and FAA advisory circulars [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].

bullets: The FAA places full responsibility for student flight training on the CFI, whom the PHAK calls the cornerstone of aviation safety [[1:38|PHAK 1-23]].

The PHAK lists CFI duties: orient the student to scenario-based training, help the student become a confident planner, inflight manager and critical evaluator of their own performance, diagnose learning difficulties, evaluate progress and keep records, and provide continuous review [[1:35|PHAK 1-20]].
Stay current and proficient in the aircraft you use, and encourage each pilot to keep 'raising the bar' [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].

Physiological obstacles: unfamiliar noise, vibration, G sensations or an uneasy stomach. Do not ignore or ridicule them; explain their causes. A sick learner may not have the capacity to learn [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].

Before solo, make sure the learner is consistent at takeoffs and landings, keeping aircraft control as the priority, proficiency in flight, traffic pattern operation, navigation and radio communication, and knows to ask ATC for help [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].

Give adequate ground and flight instruction on every ACS item. Common emphasis items include positive exchange of flight controls, stall and spin awareness, collision avoidance, runway incursion avoidance, CFIT, ADM and risk management, checklist usage and wire strike avoidance [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].
Keep a current library, follow procedures the way the FAA prescribes, and when you need help, ask a more experienced instructor, a DPE or the local FSDO [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].

callout.text: Model the behavior. Before flight discuss safety and the checklist; in flight prioritize aviate, navigate, communicate; on landing fly stabilized approaches; after flight review the choices made using ADM principles [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

check.q: Who decides a learner is ready to solo?
check.a: The AIH says it should be a joint decision between learner and instructor, generally made after the learner performs consistently from preflight to shutdown without help [[25:163|AIH 8-5]]. The endorsement itself is the instructor's call [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

body.p: The ACS adds supervision and surveillance during training. The AIH calls it pilot supervision: you provide guidance and restraint over your learners' solo operations, which it calls by far the most important flight instructor responsibility. You are the only person in a position to decide a learner is ready for solo, and before a solo endorsement you should require consistent ability on all the fundamental maneuvers [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].
Supervision with you aboard:

bullets: Brief the exchange of flight controls before flight, and use the three-step exchange every time. Numerous accidents have come from confusion over who had control, especially between learners and instructors [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

Guard the controls. When you need them, take them and calmly announce 'I have the flight controls.' Anxious learners can be incredibly strong, and there is nothing to gain from fighting them for control [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Never let a learner exceed your limits, and do not exceed your own ability to perceive a problem, decide and physically react [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Judge how much control to use. Be ready to take over on hazardous or difficult maneuvers, especially first attempts, but avoid needless interruptions when progress is normal [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

See and avoid: if learners believe you do all the scanning, they never build the habit. In one midair collision study, a flight instructor was on board in 37 percent of the accidents [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

body.p: Supervision from the ground:

bullets: First solo: be present to answer questions, and choose a time of day with traffic, winds, sun angle and reflection in mind [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].
Have a portable radio if possible so you can end the solo if a problem develops. Keep calls to a minimum and do not talk to the learner on short final [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].
Require full stop landings on the first solo; it gives you the chance to stop the flight if needed [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].
Debrief right after the solo, while the flight is vivid and questions come quickly [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

callout.text: Two veteran tips from the AIH: 'Just because it's legal, doesn't make it safe. Maintain a high level of supervision of pilot training operations,' and find a mentor for a second opinion before critical phases such as first solo [[25:165|AIH 8-7]].

check.q: What do you say, and do, when your learner hands the airplane back to you?
check.a: The learner says 'You have the flight controls,' you answer 'I have the flight controls,' and the learner keeps flying until you say it. A visual check is recommended [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

chunks.title: Supervision on paper: endorsements, recommendations and records

body.p: Much of your supervision happens with a pen. Each signature says you saw enough to know. The regulations set the minimum:

head: Rule
What it requires of you
rows: Solo endorsement
Only after you gave the required training and found the student prepared to fly safely under known circumstances, with any limitations you think necessary [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(d)(1)]]
Solo cross-country
Only after you find the student's preparation, planning, equipment and procedures adequate for that flight under the existing conditions [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(d)(2)]]
Class B solo
Only after ground and flight training in that Class B airspace or at that airport, and a finding of proficiency [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(d)(3)]]
90-day limit
A student solos only with an endorsement for that make and model from an instructor who gave the training within the 90 days before the flight [[60:277|14 CFR 61.87(n)]]
Practical test endorsement

Certifies training logged within 2 calendar months before the month of application, readiness for the test, and satisfactory knowledge of the areas missed on the knowledge test [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(6)]]
Records
Sign the logbook of everyone you train. Keep names and dates of solo endorsements, and the kind, date and result of each test you endorse, for at least 3 years [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189]]
No self-endorsement
You may not endorse yourself for any certificate, rating, flight review, authorization, practical test or knowledge test [[60:349|14 CFR 61.195(i)]]

body.p: Practical test recommendations carry a serious responsibility. Before you sign, require the applicant to thoroughly demonstrate the knowledge and skill for the certificate, never less than the complete ACS procedure [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. Endorsements need not match AC 61-65 word for word, but each must cite the part 61 section completed [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. FAA inspectors and DPEs rely on your recommendation as evidence the applicant is qualified [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

callout.text: Endorsing a learner for solo or a rating without meeting the regulations is a serious deficiency in performance. The FAA may hold that instructor accountable, and it is a breach of faith with the learner [[25:184|AIH 9-14]].
Document all training events as though the NTSB were going to read them [[25:165|AIH 8-7]].

check.q: Can you sign a solo cross-country endorsement without reviewing the learner's planning for that flight?
check.a: No. You first determine that the planning, preparation, equipment and procedures are adequate for the flight under existing conditions [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(d)(2)]].

body.p: Flight instructor qualifications start with 14 CFR 61.183. To be eligible you must be at least 18, read, speak, write and understand English, and hold a commercial or ATP certificate with the right category and class and, for an airplane single-engine instructor rating, an instrument rating [[60:339|14 CFR 61.183]]. You also need the fundamentals of instructing endorsement and knowledge tests, an endorsement on the areas of operation, the practical test, the spin training endorsement for airplanes, and 15 hours as PIC in the category and class [[60:339|14 CFR 61.183]] [[60:340|14 CFR 61.183(j)]].
Once certificated, you work within limits and privileges:

bullets: No more than 8 hours of flight training in any 24 consecutive hours [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(a)]].
To give flight training in an aircraft, hold a flight instructor certificate and a pilot certificate with that category and class rating [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(b)]].

Privileges include ground training, flight training, certain checking events and endorsements for certificates, ratings, flight reviews and tests, plus accepting a student pilot application and verifying identity and eligibility [[60:345|14 CFR 61.193]].

body.p: The AIH adds qualifications no regulation measures. Be thoroughly familiar with the function and proper use of every instrument, avionics unit and system you train with, which matters more with today's wide variety of GPS and glass displays [[25:165|AIH 8-7]]. Keep up with current training techniques and certification requirements through publications, contacts with FAA inspectors and DPEs, and clinics such as the FAASTeam/SAFE Flight Instructor Open Forums [[25:165|AIH 8-7]]. Continued use of outmoded procedures or obsolete requirements usually involves rationalization [[25:165|AIH 8-7]].

Good teachers also have four essential skills: people skills, subject matter expertise, assessment skills and management skills [[25:104|AIH 5-1]]. Management includes supervising learners, such as overseeing the preflight [[25:106|AIH 5-3]].

check.q: You hold a CFI with an airplane single-engine rating. Can you endorse your own flight review?
check.a: No. A flight instructor may not make any self-endorsement, including for a flight review [[60:349|14 CFR 61.195(i)]].

chunks.title: Professionalism: how a professional instructor acts

body.p: The aviation instructor is the central figure in aviation training and is responsible for all phases of required training. Professionals keep the highest level of knowledge, training and currency, and being a professional also means behaving in a professional manner [[25:165|AIH 8-7]]. Figure 8-7 is the AIH checklist [[25:165|AIH 8-7]] [[25:166|AIH 8-8]].

head: Trait
What the AIH expects
rows: Sincerity

Be straightforward and honest at all times. Hiding inadequacy behind a smokescreen of unrelated instruction costs the learner's respect, and any facade of pretentiousness costs confidence [[25:166|AIH 8-8]]
Acceptance of the learner

Accept learners as they are, faults and all; both of you are working toward the same objective [[25:166|AIH 8-8]]. Never degrade the learner: acceptance rather than ridicule, support rather than reproof [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]
Personal appearance and habits
Be neat, clean and appropriately dressed. Common courtesy is perhaps the most important habit, and body odor or bad breath distract in a small cockpit [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]
Demeanor

Calm, thoughtful and disciplined. Avoid contradictory directions, reacting differently to the same error at different times, unreasonable demands, unfair criticism, and an overbearing or flippant manner [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]
Proper language
Profanity and obscene language lead to distrust. Speak normally, positively and descriptively [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]

body.p: Criticizing a learner who does not learn rapidly is, in the AIH's words, like a doctor reprimanding a patient who does not get well as fast as predicted [[25:167|AIH 8-9]].

callout.text: Learners imitate your habits whether they mean to or not. Your safety talk means little if you do not demonstrate it consistently, so emphasize safety by example [[25:164|AIH 8-6]]. The PHAK adds that students watch your flying habits during lessons and when you fly for yourself [[1:38|PHAK 1-23]].

check.q: Last week you shrugged at a late flare; today you scold the same error. Which professional trait slipped?
check.a: Demeanor. The AIH says to avoid reacting differently to similar or identical errors at different times [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]; it is also a frustration rule: be consistent [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

body.p: Professional development never ends. Aviation changes rapidly, and instructors have to keep developing their knowledge and skills to teach well [[25:168|AIH 8-10]]. Successful instructors do not become complacent with their own qualifications. Learners see you as a source of up-to-date information, so you have a chance and a duty to bring new procedures to them and to other professionals [[25:168|AIH 8-10]].

head: Source
Examples from the AIH
rows: Government
FAA safety seminars, regulations, ACs, ADs, orders and notices at faa.gov, the Pilot Proficiency Awards Program, the Gold Seal certificate, and FIRCs [[25:168|AIH 8-10]]
Educational institutions
Community colleges, technical schools and universities, with degree programs or single courses [[25:169|AIH 8-11]]
Commercial organizations
Training materials and courses such as mountain flying, spin training, upset prevention and recovery and tailwheel qualification; adding category and class ratings [[25:169|AIH 8-11]]
Industry organizations
Membership in groups such as SAFE and NAFI [[25:165|AIH 8-7]]; local chapters, safety symposiums and training clinics [[25:169|AIH 8-11]]
Sources of material
Current regulations, the AIM, the ACS and pilot training manuals, in print or electronic form [[25:169|AIH 8-11]] [[25:170|AIH 8-12]]

body.p: The rules also require you to stay active. You may exercise instructor privileges only if, within the preceding 24 calendar months, you met one recent experience option [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(a)]]:

bullets: Pass a flight instructor practical test for a rating you hold or an additional rating [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(b)(1)]].
Endorse at least 5 applicants for practical tests with at least 80 percent passing on the first attempt [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(b)(2)(i)]].

Serve as a company check pilot, chief flight instructor, check airman or flight instructor in a part 121 or 135 operation, or in a position involving the regular evaluation of pilots [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(b)(2)(ii)]].
Complete an approved FIRC within the preceding 3 calendar months [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(b)(2)(iii)]].

body.p: If you miss it, you may not instruct until privileges are reinstated. More than 3 calendar months late means a flight instructor practical test [[60:352|14 CFR 61.199(a)]]. A Gold Seal certificate needs, within the previous 24 calendar months, at least 10 applicants trained and recommended with at least 80 percent passing first time, or 20 practical tests as a DPE, or a mix where two tests count as one applicant [[12:24|AC 61-65K 28]].

check.q: Name two reasons the AIH gives for keeping a supply of current publications.
check.a: Fresh material keeps instruction interesting and up to date, and it keeps you informed about what is being written in aviation [[25:169|AIH 8-11]].

body.p: Instructor ethics and conduct start with what you are building. The aviation instructor has the added duty of molding an aviation citizen, a pilot who is an asset to the aviation community [[25:106|AIH 5-3]]. The AIH's instructor's code of ethics says you are teaching a pilot who should [[25:106|AIH 5-3]] [[25:107|AIH 5-4]]:

bullets: Make safety the number one priority, develop and exercise good judgment, and recognize and manage risk [[25:106|AIH 5-3]].
Be accountable, act with responsibility and courtesy, and keep to prudent practices, personal operating parameters, laws and regulations [[25:106|AIH 5-3]].
Seek proficiency in aircraft control, use flight deck technology safely, be confident in many situations, and respect the privilege of flight [[25:107|AIH 5-4]].

body.p: These ideas are part of the Flight Instructors Model Code of Conduct (FIMCC), built by a diverse team of aviation professionals and widely peer reviewed. A formal code promotes safety, good judgment, ethical behavior and personal responsibility, all parts of professionalism. The FIMCC, the Aviator's Model Code of Conduct and a Student Pilot's Model Code are at secureav.com, and NAFI and SAFE post codes of ethics too [[25:107|AIH 5-4]].

The Aviator's Model Code of Conduct gives GA pilots guidance in seven sections: general responsibilities, passengers and people on the surface, training and proficiency, security, environmental issues, use of technology, and advancement of general aviation. Its principles complement and supplement what is merely legal, and it is not meant to be a standard [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].
Conduct in practice:

bullets: Regulations alone do not guarantee safety; new combinations of circumstances arise that no rule foresaw, so be proactive [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].

If you believe a learner may have a serious psychological abnormality, stop instructing that learner, have an unacquainted instructor fly an evaluation flight, and withhold solo endorsements and test recommendations if you both agree [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].
Know the learner's background, credentials, security issues and medications before climbing into the cockpit together [[25:165|AIH 8-7]].

check.q: Is the Aviator's Model Code of Conduct a regulation you can be violated under?
check.a: No. It is not a standard; it complements and supplements what is merely legal [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].

chunks.title: Risks: falling short on responsibilities or professionalism

body.p: Two risks run through this Task: not fulfilling instructor responsibilities (R1) and not exhibiting professionalism (R2). The sources show what each looks like and what stops it.

head: Risk
What can happen
Mitigation
rows: Training to pass the test only
The RMH says about 85 percent of accidents in the last 20 years were caused by pilot error, and many come from training aimed at passing tests while risk management is ignored [[30:4|RMH ii]]
Integrate risk management into training [[30:4|RMH ii]]; teach why and when, not only how [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]
Careless endorsement or recommendation
A serious deficiency; the FAA may hold you accountable; a breach of faith with the learner [[25:184|AIH 9-14]]
Require consistent performance and the complete ACS procedure first [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]
Unclear control exchange
Accidents from confusion about who had control [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Brief and use the three-step exchange [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]
Learner relies on you to scan
The learner never develops constant vigilance [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]
Correct any entry into a maneuver without a clearing check at once [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]
Falling behind
Technology can outpace an instructor's knowledge [[25:49|AIH 2-16]]; outmoded procedures persist through rationalization [[25:165|AIH 8-7]]
Continuing education and current sources [[25:170|AIH 8-12]]
Unprofessional behavior
Lost respect and confidence, and learners copy what they see [[25:166|AIH 8-8]] [[25:164|AIH 8-6]]
Follow the Do's and Don'ts and teach safety by example [[25:166|AIH 8-8]] [[25:164|AIH 8-6]]
Lapsed recent experience
You may not exercise instructor privileges [[60:352|14 CFR 61.197(c)]]
Track your 24 calendar month period [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(a)]]

callout.text: The flight instructor's primary legal responsibility is the decision whether to endorse a learner for solo or recommend a practical test [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].

check.q: Which handbook warns that training aimed only at passing tests leaves risk management out?

body.p: S1 has the examiner assign a Task and watch you deliver it in a way that matches K1 to K5. A simple flow built from this lesson's sources:

bullets: Before: arrive early and prepared, with time planned for the unexpected [[25:105|AIH 5-2]]. State the objective and the standard [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]. In flight lessons, brief the exchange of controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

During: define common terms and remember the learner is new to aviation jargon [[25:166|AIH 8-8]]. Give credit when due and criticize constructively [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]. Stay calm and consistent [[25:167|AIH 8-9]].

After: keep the learner informed of progress with written notes, point out where each deficiency began, and suggest a correction [[25:168|AIH 8-10]]. Assign specific homework and document the lesson [[25:165|AIH 8-7]].

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Teaching to the minimum
'Within ACS limits, good enough' on an early lesson
Build lesson standards that reach or exceed the ACS and explain why the standards exist [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]
One method for everyone
The CFI teaches every learner the way they were taught
Analyze each learner and adapt [[25:159|AIH 8-1]] [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]
Inventing errors
A fast learner gets nitpicked to stay humble
Raise the standard instead; unfair criticism destroys confidence [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]
Praise for everything
'Great job' after every attempt
Praise when deserved; free praise becomes valueless [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Correction with no explanation
'No, again'
Explain what went wrong and how to fix it [[25:162|AIH 8-4]] [[25:166|AIH 8-8]]
Bluffing an answer
A vague reply to a question you cannot answer
Admit it, research it and get back to the learner [[25:162|AIH 8-4]] [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]
Fear-based first lesson
Accident stories before the learner knows normal flight
Start with normal operations [[25:161|AIH 8-3]]
Chatty solo supervision
Radio calls to a solo learner on short final
Keep calls to a minimum and silent on short final [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]

check.q: During a practice ground lesson your friend asks a question you cannot answer. What does a professional do?
check.a: Admit it, research the answer and get back to the learner. Bluffing is sensed quickly and destroys confidence [[25:162|AIH 8-4]] [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

activities.title: Which responsibility is it?
activities.intro: Tap an action, then the instructor responsibility it shows best.

items.t: Keeping lessons enjoyable without lowering the bar
Telling the learner today's lesson objective
Talking at length about a new learner's background and temperament
Teaching S-turns with headings first, then altitude and drift
Training every task to the ACS for the certificate sought
Raising lesson completion standards until they meet the ACS
Making the first flight a normal trip to a nearby airport
Saving emergencies until normal operations are familiar
Giving a week's notice of the stage check
Admitting you gave a wrong pattern altitude last lesson

activities.title: Additional flight instructor duties
activities.intro: Drag each description to the numbered pin on the duty it describes.

pins.label: Judging a maneuver against standards suited to the learner's stage
Guidance and restraint over solo operations
Signing the application only after the full ACS procedure is shown
Logbook sign-offs that must cite the part 61 section
Staying current in your aircraft and helping pilots raise the bar
Making sure the learner, not just you, keeps the lookout

activities.title: Teaching a new maneuver with the controls
activities.intro: Put the AIH sequence for sharing the controls on a new maneuver in order.
steps: On the ground, brief the procedure for exchanging the flight controls
The learner follows along on the controls during a demonstration
The learner performs the maneuver with the instructor following along

activities.title: Match the trait to the behavior
activities.intro: Tap a professional trait, then the behavior that shows it.

pairs.r: Does not hide a gap in knowledge behind unrelated talk
Supports a slow learner instead of reproving him
Reacts the same way to the same error every time
Speaks positively and descriptively, without profanity
Uses the practices she teaches even when no learner is watching

activities.title: Numbers a working CFI uses
activities.intro: Work it out from the rule, then type your answer.

items.q: In the current 24 consecutive hours you have given 3.2 hours and 2.5 hours of flight training. How many more hours of flight training may you give in that period?
items.why: Limit 8 hours in any 24 consecutive hours: 8 - (3.2 + 2.5) = 8 - 5.7 = 2.3 hours [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(a)]].

items.q: To use your pass rate for recent experience, you endorsed 7 applicants in 24 calendar months. At least how many must have passed on the first attempt?
items.why: At least 80 percent: 0.80 x 7 = 5.6, so at least 6 must pass (5 would be only 71 percent). You also need at least 5 endorsed [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(b)(2)(i)]].

items.q: Gold Seal: you trained and recommended 6 applicants. How many practical tests as a DPE would make up the rest of the 10-applicant credit?
items.why: Two practical tests count as one applicant: (10 - 6) x 2 = 8 tests [[12:24|AC 61-65K 28]].

items.q: You endorsed a student for solo on January 10 and she plans a solo on April 15 of the same year. How many days is that? (If more than 90, she needs a new endorsement.)
items.why: 21 days left in January + 28 in February + 31 in March + 15 in April = 95 days, more than the 90 days the rule allows [[60:277|14 CFR 61.87(n)]].

items.q: You have held your CFI for 30 calendar months and have given 143 hours of flight training. Using the hours route, how many more hours must you give before you may train initial airplane CFI applicants?
items.why: The route requires 24 calendar months as a CFI and at least 200 hours of flight training given: 200 - 143 = 57 hours [[60:347|14 CFR 61.195(h)(2)(i)(A)]].

activities.title: True or false: ethics and conduct
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The Aviator's Model Code of Conduct is a standard pilots are tested against.
cards.why: False. It is not a standard and is not meant to be implemented as one [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].

cards.s: The FIMCC was developed by a diverse team and peer reviewed in the aviation community.
If a flight is legal, the instructor's safety judgment is finished.
cards.why: False. Even strict compliance with regulations may not guarantee safety [[25:164|AIH 8-6]], and 'just because it's legal, doesn't make it safe' [[25:165|AIH 8-7]].

cards.s: Endorsing a learner who does not meet the regulations is a breach of faith with that learner.
A CFI may endorse his own flight review.
The instructor's code says to teach a pilot who keeps to personal operating parameters.

activities.title: A new CFI's first learner, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are a new CFI. Alex, a learner pilot with no flight time, books lessons with you at a busy part 61 school.

steps.s: Lesson one. What flight do you plan?
options: A stall demonstration so Alex respects the airplane
A simulated engine failure to show how serious flying is
A normal flight to a nearby airport and back
A ground-only lesson on accident statistics
steps.why: The AIH's positive first lesson is a normal flight to a nearby airport; stalls and emergencies come after normal operations are familiar [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

steps.s: Lesson six. Alex asks a regulation question and you are not sure of the answer.
options: Give your best guess confidently
Change the subject
Say you are not sure, look it up and get back to Alex
Tell Alex it will not be on the test
steps.why: Admit errors and doubt; bluffing is sensed quickly [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]. Research the answer and get back to the learner [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

steps.s: Lesson fourteen. Alex flies from preflight to shutdown consistently with no help from you.
options: Endorse and send Alex solo right now without discussion
Talk it over with Alex, then endorse only if you judge Alex ready
Wait until Alex passes the private ACS standards
Ask another learner to decide
steps.why: Solo readiness should be a joint decision, made when the learner performs consistently without help [[25:163|AIH 8-5]]. The endorsement is yours, after the required training and your finding that Alex can fly safely [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(d)(1)]].

steps.s: Solo day. The schedule shows the busiest hour of the afternoon with a low sun on final.
options: Keep the slot; Alex has to learn traffic sometime
Move the solo to a quieter time with better wind and sun angle
Fly it, but talk Alex through every leg on the radio
Send Alex solo while you teach another lesson
steps.why: Consider time of day for traffic, winds, sun angle and reflection, and be present for the first solo [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

steps.s: Alex is on short final, a little high but correcting.
options: Radio a correction now
Stay quiet and let Alex fly
Tell Alex to go around immediately
Ask the tower to relay advice
steps.why: Keep radio calls to a minimum and do not talk to the learner on short final [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. You taught go-arounds for a bad approach before solo [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

scenario.title: Six weeks into your CFI career
scenario.setup: You earned your CFI six weeks ago and teach at a busy part 61 school. This week: Maria (25 hours) lands well but waves off small errors and says she is basically ready to solo. Dan (18 hours) is quiet and hesitates to call go-arounds even when he sees the problem. A renter you have never flown with asks you to 'just sign' his flight review because he flew a lot last month. Late on Thursday you have already given 6.1 hours of dual when a learner asks for a 2-hour lesson. During ground school, a learner asks about a GPS mode you do not know. And the scheduler has put Maria's first solo at the busiest hour of the day.

questions.a: Fast learners can become overconfident. Raise the standard each lesson and demand more effort, make her aware of her errors, but do not invent any [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]. Solo comes when she performs consistently, as a joint decision, with your endorsement [[25:163|AIH 8-5]] [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

Do not mistake reserve for slow learning. Aim instruction at self-confidence rather than more drill [[25:159|AIH 8-1]], use easier goals built element by element [[25:160|AIH 8-2]], and give credit when due [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

questions.q: What do you tell the renter?
questions.a: You may not endorse a flight review unless you conducted the review required by 61.56(a) [[60:347|14 CFR 61.195(d)(5)]]. Signing anyway would be a breach of faith and the FAA may hold you accountable [[25:184|AIH 9-14]].

questions.q: Can you fly the 2-hour lesson Thursday night?
questions.a: Not if it falls within the same 24 consecutive hours: 6.1 + 2.0 = 8.1 hours, over the 8-hour limit on flight training [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(a)]]. Shorten it to 1.9 hours or less, or reschedule.

questions.q: How do you answer the GPS question?
questions.a: Admit you do not know, find out and get back to the learner [[25:162|AIH 8-4]] [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]. Then fix the gap: instructors need thorough familiarity with the avionics they train with [[25:165|AIH 8-7]].

questions.q: What do you change about Maria's solo?
questions.a: Pick a time of day with less traffic and good winds and sun angle, be present with a radio, keep calls minimal and silent on short final [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], and require full stop landings [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

skills.do: Deliver ground or flight instruction on an evaluator-assigned Task in a manner consistent with instructor responsibilities and professional characteristics as stated in K1 through K5 (ACS FI.I.E.S1). The examiner picks a Task and watches you teach it: stating the objective and standard, adapting to the 'learner' (often the examiner role-playing), praising and correcting constructively, staying calm and consistent, admitting what you do not know, and briefing the exchange of controls in flight.
skills.practice: Have a friend pick a Task at random from the private ACS and give you 10 minutes to prepare. Teach it while they play a quiet, a fast or a frustrated learner. Afterward score yourself against the Instructor Do's and Don'ts [[25:166|AIH 8-8]] and the seven frustration rules [[25:162|AIH 8-4]], and rehearse briefings on video until delivery is polished [[25:165|AIH 8-7]].

quiz.q: In one line, what does the AIH say the job of an aviation instructor is?
options: To pass applicants on the first attempt
To transfer knowledge
To enforce regulations
To fly as safety pilot
quiz.why: The job of an aviation instructor is to transfer knowledge [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

quiz.q: The AIH describes the ACS/PTS as:
options: A teaching document
A syllabus
A testing document, not a teaching document
A list of minimum lesson standards
quiz.why: It should be emphasized that the ACS/PTS is a testing document, not a teaching document [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

quiz.q: What does the AIH say to do with a fast learner who makes few mistakes?
options: Leave them alone
Invent deficiencies so they stay humble
Constantly raise the standard for each lesson
Move them straight to the checkride
quiz.why: Constantly raise the standard of performance and demand greater effort; never invent deficiencies [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

quiz.q: What happens to praise that is given too freely?
options: It becomes valueless
It builds overconfidence only in slow learners
It speeds up solo
It replaces critique
quiz.why: Praise pays dividends when deserved, but given too freely it becomes valueless [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

quiz.q: Which responsibility does the AIH call by far the most important for a flight instructor?
options: Keeping a current library
Pilot supervision of solo operations
Assigning homework
Joining a professional organization
quiz.why: Guidance and restraint over learners' solo operations is by far the most important flight instructor responsibility [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

quiz.q: What does the AIH say about talking to a learner during a supervised solo?
options: Coach every leg
Talk only on short final
Keep calls to a minimum and do not talk on short final
Never carry a radio
quiz.why: Keep radio communications to a minimum and do not talk to the learner on short final [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

quiz.q: Before endorsing a student for solo, the instructor must have given the required training and determined the student:
options: Has passed the knowledge test
Is prepared to conduct the flight safely under known circumstances
Holds a medical
Has 10 hours

quiz.q: Which is a demeanor fault the AIH tells instructors to avoid?
options: Speaking descriptively
Reacting differently to identical errors at different times
Accepting a learner's faults
Admitting mistakes
quiz.why: Avoid contradictory directions and reacting differently to similar or identical errors at different times [[25:167|AIH 8-9]].

quiz.q: Which professional organizations does the AIH name for flight instructors?
options: SAFE and NAFI
ICAO and IATA
NTSB and TSA
ALPA and NBAA
quiz.why: The AIH names the Society of Aviation and Flight Educators and the National Association of Flight Instructors [[25:165|AIH 8-7]].

quiz.q: How many sections does the Aviator's Model Code of Conduct have?
options: Five
Seven
Ten
Fourteen
quiz.why: It has seven sections, from general responsibilities of aviators to advancement and promotion of general aviation [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].

final_quiz.q: During a steep turn your learner freezes and resists your input. What does the AIH say?
options: Keep both of you on the controls and push harder
Calmly announce 'I have the flight controls' and take them; nothing is gained by fighting the learner
Talk the learner through it without touching the controls
Pull the power and wait
final_quiz.why: Take the controls and calmly announce 'I have the flight controls.' Anxious learners can be very strong, and there is nothing to gain from fighting for control [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your applicant missed several areas on the knowledge test. What must your practical test endorsement certify about them?
options: Nothing; the DPE handles them
That the applicant retook the knowledge test
That the applicant has demonstrated satisfactory knowledge of those areas
That the applicant read the ACS
final_quiz.why: The endorsement certifies satisfactory knowledge of the subject areas missed on the knowledge test [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(6)(iii)]]. Recommendations also show those areas were reviewed [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

final_quiz.q: Your recent experience period ends in June. You finish a FIRC in March. From when does your next 24 calendar month period run?
options: From March, the month of the FIRC
From June, the last month of the current period
From the original issue month
From January of the next year
final_quiz.why: If the requirement is met within the 3 calendar months preceding the last month of the current period, the new period starts from that last month [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(a)(3)]] [[12:26|AC 61-65K 30.3]].

final_quiz.q: On her first flight, a learner feels queasy in the turns and apologizes. The professional response is to:
options: Joke about it to lighten the mood
Ignore it and finish the lesson plan
Explain the cause of the sensation and adjust; a sick learner may not be able to learn
Tell her flying may not be for her
final_quiz.why: Do not ignore or ridicule physiological obstacles; understanding their causes usually overcomes them, and a sick learner may lack the capacity to learn [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].

final_quiz.q: You teach a ground school of twelve and pitch everything at the 'typical' student. Which frustration rule are you breaking?
options: Be consistent
Approach learners as individuals
Admit errors
Give credit when due
final_quiz.why: Thinking only of the whole group aims at an average personality that fits no one [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

final_quiz.q: After a poor approach you say only 'That was unsatisfactory.' What does the AIH predict?
options: Faster improvement from the shock
Frustration, and errors that continue through faulty practice
Better retention
Nothing, as long as you are consistent
final_quiz.why: Telling an earnest learner the work is unsatisfactory with no explanation causes frustration, and unidentified errors are perpetuated through faulty practice [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner sees you skip the before-takeoff checklist on your own flight. Why does this matter most?
options: It is a violation the learner must report
Learners imitate their instructor's habits, so your talk on safety loses meaning
It only matters on checkrides
It does not matter if you are proficient
final_quiz.why: Learners treat the instructor as a role model and imitate habits; advocacy means little without consistent example [[25:164|AIH 8-6]] [[1:38|PHAK 1-23]].

final_quiz.q: Before you sign a private pilot practical test recommendation, the applicant should demonstrate:
options: The maneuvers they find hardest
A random sample of tasks
No less than the complete procedure in the ACS
A mock oral only
final_quiz.why: The demonstration should in no instance be less than the complete procedure prescribed in the ACS/PTS [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

final_quiz.q: You want to word an endorsement differently from the AC 61-65 sample. Is that acceptable?
options: No, it must match word for word
Yes, but it must at least cite the part 61 section completed
Yes, any wording works
Only with FSDO approval
final_quiz.why: Endorsements need not be worded exactly as in AC 61-65, but at a minimum must cite the appropriate part 61 section [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

final_quiz.q: A learner shows extreme mood swings and you suspect a serious psychological problem. The AIH says to first:
options: Solo the learner to build confidence
Have an instructor who does not know the learner fly an evaluation flight, then confer
Report the learner to the TSA
Keep instructing and say nothing
final_quiz.why: Arrange an evaluation flight by an unacquainted instructor, confer, and withhold endorsements if warranted [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].

final_quiz.q: Your school adds an airplane with an avionics suite you have never used. Before you instruct in it, the AIH says you need:
options: Nothing; basic flying skills transfer
Thorough familiarity with its instruments, avionics and systems
A new CFI practical test
A type rating
final_quiz.why: A flight instructor needs to be thoroughly familiar with the function and proper use of all instruments, avionics and systems used for training [[25:165|AIH 8-7]].

final_quiz.q: A former learner asks for a solo endorsement for a Class B airport where you have never trained her. You may endorse her only after:
options: Reviewing a video of that airport
Giving her ground and flight training at that airport and finding her proficient
She passes a knowledge test
She flies there with any pilot
final_quiz.why: Solo at an airport within Class B requires your ground and flight training there and a finding of proficiency [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(d)(3)]].

final_quiz.q: A learner says, 'Once I pass the checkride, I'm a finished pilot.' What does the PHAK say you should stress?
options: That the checkride covers everything
That practical tests are a sampling of ability, and your goal is the total pilot
That the ACS is the full syllabus
That more training is only for professionals
final_quiz.why: Practical tests are a sampling of pilot ability compressed into a short period; the goal is to train the 'total' pilot [[1:39|PHAK 1-24]].

takeaways: Five instructor responsibilities: help learners, give adequate instruction, train to standards, emphasize the positive, minimize frustration.
Tailor instruction to the learner: build confidence in the timid, raise the bar for the fast.
The ACS is a testing document; build lesson standards up to and past it.
Pilot supervision of solo operations is the most important flight instructor duty.
Every endorsement and recommendation is a judgment you are accountable for; meet the rule and document it.
Professionalism is sincerity, acceptance, appearance, calm demeanor and clean language, plus safety by example.
Keep learning, and keep your 24 calendar month recent experience current.
cfi_notes: The ACS K1 list and AIH Figure 8-1 differ: the figure shows 'demanding appropriate standards' and 'ensuring aviation safety' while the ACS says 'training to established standards' and 'minimizing learner frustrations' [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]. The AIH text headings match the ACS [[25:159|AIH 8-1]] [[25:160|AIH 8-2]] [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]. Teach the ACS list and mention the figure.

The AIH says the instructor's 8710-1 signature 'is valid for 60 days' [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. The regulation says the endorsement certifies training logged within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(6)(i)]]. Teach the CFR wording.

The AIH describes FIRCs as meeting the training requirements for 'renewal of flight instructor certificates' [[25:168|AIH 8-10]]. Current 61.197 uses recent experience within 24 calendar months; renewal before expiration applies only to certificates issued before December 1, 2024 [[60:351|14 CFR 61.197(a)]] [[60:352|14 CFR 61.197(e)]]. Teach the CFR terms.

The ACS says 'supervision and surveillance'; the AIH uses 'pilot supervision' and never defines surveillance [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. Treat surveillance as the ongoing watching you do before and after solo: endorsement reviews, first solo oversight and post-solo debriefs [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

The AIH says solo readiness should be a joint decision [[25:163|AIH 8-5]] and also that the instructor is the only person in a position to make it [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. Involve the learner, but the call and the signature are yours [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(d)(1)]].

Expect the examiner to role-play a difficult learner during S1. Name what you see (timid, overconfident, frustrated) and answer with the AIH remedy [[25:159|AIH 8-1]] [[25:160|AIH 8-2]] [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].
Use the veteran tips in Figure 8-6 as habits: a mentor's second opinion before first solos, homework after each flight, and documentation as if the NTSB will read it [[25:165|AIH 8-7]].
When you do not know an answer, the AIH wants the admission, the research and the follow-up, and better yet, enough extra knowledge to answer the first time [[25:162|AIH 8-4]] [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].
The AIH 'Correction of learner errors' and collaborative assessment topics belong to FI.I.B and FI.I.D; this Task only needs them as part of constructive criticism [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].
gaps: Figure 8-5 lists 'additional training and endorsements' and 'learner's pre-solo flight thought process' [[25:163|AIH 8-5]], but the AIH gives no separate text on them. Use AC 61-65K and your syllabus.
No source here gives a method or schedule for monitoring a solo learner after the first solo beyond the endorsement rules [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(d)]]. Set it with your school's procedures.
The AIH asks for appropriate attire [[25:167|AIH 8-9]] but sets no dress standard; follow your school's policy.
The FIMCC and the Aviator's Model Code are only summarized in the AIH [[25:107|AIH 5-4]] [[25:164|AIH 8-6]]; read their full text at the source the AIH names.
Part 61 limits flight training to 8 hours in 24 consecutive hours [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(a)]] but sets no limit on ground training or total duty day. Personal limits are CFI judgment.
